title: Silent quota exhaustion: detection, mitigation and follow-up notes
body:
Executive summary:

On 2026-02-15 we observed a gradual but sustained rise in token consumption and 99p latency for the public text-generation API across US-WEST and EU-WEST over ~12 hours. The event did not trigger obvious abuse alarms because traffic per-API-key stayed under hard limits; the effective problem was 'silent quota exhaustion' where many clients simultaneously exercised retries and a misconfigured downstream library caused exponential token usage. A leaked service key (limited-scope) was discovered as an amplifying vector — automated agents using that key retried aggressively, causing a large number of high-cost generation calls. In parallel, a temporary WAF tightening (rule batch-rollout) blocked our internal admin revoke endpoint from certain regions, slowing key revocation.

Impact highlights:
- Token burn rate increased ~4x from baseline (estimated peak ~42M tokens/hour).
- 99p latency increased from ~210ms to ~760ms for text-generation endpoints in US-WEST and EU-WEST.
- Customer-facing rate-limits were hit for several enterprise tenants; two dedicated capacity pools reported degraded throughput due to upstream throttling.
- No data exfiltration detected; the leaked key had read-write but limited project scope.

Timeline (local times):
- 2026-02-15 02:10: early anomaly: token rate +30% sustained over 10m (internal alert).
- 2026-02-15 02:20: 99p latency starts rising in US-WEST; oncall acked.
- 2026-02-15 03:05: automated abuse detection (rate-pattern matcher) flagged many low-cardinality API keys with unusual retry signatures; signal suppressed by low individual RPS threshold.
- 2026-02-15 04:12: SRE runbook invoked; initial mitigation: temporary tighten global rate-limits to protect SLOs.
- 2026-02-15 04:30: discovered leaked service key used by third-party automation; attempted immediate revocation.
- 2026-02-15 04:45: WAF batch rule rollout blocked internal revoke endpoint from EU-WEST; revocation delayed until WAF rule rollback at 05:12.
- 2026-02-15 05:50: token burn reduces to near-baseline after key revoked and targeted throttles applied.
- 2026-02-15 07:10: follow-up mitigations and monitoring in place; incident declared mitigated.

How it evaded normal detection:
- Low-cardinality per-key usage — each abusive agent used a different key or rotated ephemeral tokens, keeping per-key RPS under thresholds.
- Traffic matched legitimate client user-agent strings (scraping clients used standard libs), so UA-based heuristics did not match.
- The exponential backoff bug in the third-party client produced long-tail bursts (many small generation requests), which increased tokens without producing large spikes in request rate metrics used by current abuse detectors.
- WAF rule change prevented our own internal tooling from doing immediate admin actions in one region.

Detection signals that ultimately helped:
- Token-per-request distribution shifted right (tokens/request median unchanged but 95p and 99p rose).
- Sudden correlation between increased failed-sample ratio in our sampler and token burn.
- New low-latency increase in KV cache churn (prefix cache misses rose) indicated many unique prefixes used by the same agent cluster.
- Cross-region correlation: US-WEST and EU-WEST both spiked within the same 30-minute window.

Queries and dashboards used (copy for runbook):
- BigQuery: tokens/hour by api_key and region (example):
  SELECT region, api_key, SUM(tokens) as tokens_hour
  FROM `prod_telemetry.tokens_agg`
  WHERE timestamp BETWEEN TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 1 HOUR) AND CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()
  GROUP BY region, api_key
  ORDER BY tokens_hour DESC

- Prometheus: high-token-per-request indicator (example):
  increase(api_request_tokens_total[1h]) / increase(api_request_count_total[1h]) > 1.5 * baseline_tokens_per_request

- KV cache churn:
  increase(kv_cache_misses_total[30m]) > 3x baseline

Immediate mitigation steps executed (what worked):
1) Scoped key revocation: revoke the leaked service key and all short-lived tokens issued by that key. (Owner: security oncall)
2) Targeted rate-limit rules: apply per-caller fingerprint limits (fingerprint created from combination of ip / agent / uncommon header patterns) rather than only per-api-key; throttled matching fingerprints to 5 rps. (Owner: SRE oncall)
3) Emergency rollback of WAF batch rule that blocked admin revoke endpoints. (Owner: infra oncall)
4) Temporary global soft-cap: decrease global per-tenant burst allowance to preserve SLOs while we triaged. (Owner: platform)

Mitigations that were attempted but problematic:
- Blanket global hard-rate limits: too disruptive to healthy workloads and enterprise customers.
- Aggressive IP blocking: many agents used cloud provider IP ranges; blocking widely would have high collateral.

Root cause analysis (working hypothesis):
- Primary cause: A third-party integration had a bug that caused it to retry non-idempotent generation calls exponentially when encountering transient downstream errors, amplifying per-call token consumption.
- Amplifier: A leaked service key that allowed many instances of the third-party agent to authenticate and generate calls.
- Operational failure: Recent WAF rule rollout inadvertently prevented internal admin actions in affected regions, delaying revocation.

Draft runbook: Silent quota exhaustion / distributed low-rate abuse (first-draft)
Purpose: provide a step-by-step for oncall to detect and mitigate multi-key low-rate abuse patterns that increase token burn and threaten latency SLOs.

Detection phase:
- If tokens/hour > 2x baseline OR 99p latency > 1.5x SLO for 30m, start this runbook.
- Run the BigQuery tokens-by-key query. If top N keys each < per-key hard limit but collectively > threshold, suspect rotational/ephemeral-key abuse.
- Check tokens/request distribution and KV cache churn metrics.

Containment phase (order matters):
1) Apply temporary per-fingerprint throttles (see fingerprint generation snippet below).
2) Reduce global tenant burst allowances to a safe default for up to 2 hours.
3) Revoke known leaked keys, prioritize service keys and keys with admin scopes.
4) If WAF rules may affect admin tooling, pause/rollback relevant WAF rule batches and confirm admin endpoints reachable from control-plane subnets.
5) Coordinate with security team to trace token issuance paths and identify token minting client ids.

Fingerprint generation (simple heuristic):
- fingerprint = sha256(normalize(ip) + normalize(user_agent) + first_32_bytes_of(x-client-id))
- Use fingerprint to group low-rate callers that look similar. Store in temporary table and run fingerprint frequency query.

Assesment & recovery:
- Once throttles + revocations reduce tokens/hour to <1.2x baseline for 45m, start controlled rollback of temporary limits.
- Re-enable burst allowances gradually with canary tenants.

Post-incident tasks (action items):
- SRE: add token-per-request and KV-cache-churn to default alerting baseline (done: ETA 2026-03-01).
- SRE + Platform: implement per-fingerprint rate limiting as a pluggable policy in the rate-limiter (RFC due 2026-03-15).
- Security: add automated scan for leaked service keys in commit history and cloud logs; integrate with key-rotation automation (ETA 2026-03-08).
- Product: examine tenant-facing SDKs and publish a best-practices doc on idempotency and retry semantics for generation calls.
- Infra: add a WAF rollout safety check: blocklist changes that prevent access to critical internal control-plane endpoints; require preflight from control-plane before rollout (ETA 2026-03-05).

Open issues and follow-ups:
- Determine how many third-party agents were responsible vs. misconfigured internal customers (investigation in SRE-1129).
- Run a replay of token costs by tenant for Feb 15 to reconcile billing impacts.
- Evaluate adding probabilistic sampling of request bodies to detect repeated prefixes/patterns used by scrapers (privacy review required).

Lessons learned (guidance for future incidents):
- Relying purely on per-key thresholds is insufficient; attackers and buggy clients can rotate keys or use ephemeral tokens to keep per-key rates low while burning resources.
- Operational tooling should be resilient to own networking/security rollout changes; preflight checks must include control-plane reachability tests.
- Fingerprinting is imperfect and must be used carefully to avoid false positives against multi-tenant clients that legitimately share infrastructure.

Owners for follow-ups:
- Add alerts + dashboards: Ethan Park (eng-sre)
- Rate-limiter fingerprinting RFC & implementation: Samir Patel (platform)
- WAF rollout safety gating: Avery Lin (infra)
